To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
grouping of visual elements into objects is accompanied by reduced activity in V1 and increased activity in LOC.

1) grouping of elements into objects is associated with a reduction of activity in V2, and 2) the reduction of activity is mediated by feedback from higher object areas (LOC) to early visual areas (V2).
activity in higher visual areas (LOC) increases when objects are grouped and activity in lower visual areas (V1) is reduced.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the interactions between cortical areas that underlie visual perception.
the interactions between cortical areas in visual perception, and we discuss the implications of our findings for understanding the role of feedback in perception.
the interactions between visual areas and how they contribute to perceptual grouping and object recognition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the visual cortex is a hierarchical network of interacting regions, with feedback from high-level areas to lower-level areas that is essential to perceptual grouping and visual perception in general.

perceptual grouping and the resulting reduction of activity in early visual cortex may be a consequence of a general mechanism for reducing uncertainty and complexity in the visual representation of a scene.
feedback is not only a means of conveying information, but also a means to simplify the description and processing of a visual image, and thus to improve the efficiency of visual processing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
perceptual grouping is not only a function of local visual processing, but also involves interactions between higher and lower visual areas.

perceptual grouping is a process of 'explaining' the visual world in a probabilistic manner, and the brain does so by reducing the complexity of visual representations in a hierarchical manner, starting from early visual areas and ending in higher visual areas.
the perceptual grouping process is a result of the interactions between visual areas, and that the LOC is a critical area for this process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
perceptual grouping processes can be understood as the result of interactions between visual cortical regions.
feedback from high to low visual areas is not just about the top down control of visual attention, but is also involved in perceptual grouping processes that are critical for object recognition.
perceptual grouping processes in higher areas are reflected in the activity of lower visual areas, and that this reflects a general principle of how the brain reduces the complexity of the world.
